segments.title: Building a super Queen Elizabeth to face an improved Bismarck
segments.body: The exercise pits a Queen Elizabeth-derived ship with five triple 16.5-inch turrets against an improved Bismarck. Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts makes the counterfactual visible through choices about hull dimensions, machinery, fire control, armour, and secondary weapons. The initial design is deliberately ambitious, and the rest of the stream tests whether its fifteen-gun broadside can become a balanced fighting ship. This premise explains the later reconstructions and battle tests.

evidence.note: He explains the viewer-suggested super Queen Elizabeth versus super-Bismarck comparison and begins laying out the 16.5-inch-gun design.

segments.summary: The stream opens by turning a viewer's counterfactual into a design contest between a heavily modernized Queen Elizabeth type and the earlier super-Bismarck model.

segments.title: What the weight budget does to a fifteen-gun battleship
segments.body: The design sequence shows how quickly a fifteen-gun main battery consumes a battleship's displacement. Belt and deck armour, barbette protection, bulkheads, torpedo defence, machinery, beam, and draft all affect weight distribution and stability. Recovering enough tonnage for a 4.5-inch secondary battery requires giving ground elsewhere. Every improvement competes for weight and space, so a workable battleship cannot maximize every characteristic at once.

evidence.note: He repeatedly trades armour, bulkheads, torpedo defence, machinery, beam, and draft against the need to fit the main and secondary batteries within displacement.

segments.summary: Fitting fifteen 16.5-inch guns forces compromises among armour, underwater protection, machinery, range, secondary guns, and hull balance.

segments.title: Fitting 4.5-inch, Bofors, and Oerlikon batteries around the main guns
segments.body: With the main battery and basic protection in place, the remaining tonnage goes to a 4.5-inch secondary battery and representations of Bofors 40 mm and Oerlikon 20 mm weapons. The game does not provide every exact mount, so nominal calibre and barrel length are adjusted to approximate the intended systems. The result is a layout exercise rather than a literal reconstruction. These smaller weapons still compete for deck space, firing arcs, and weight, and single mounts cannot fit in every desired position. The sequence shows how a modernization's anti-aircraft battery must fit around turrets and superstructure after the main-battery decisions are made.

evidence.note: He fits 4.5-inch secondaries, adds Bofors and Oerlikon representations, converts their nominal calibres and barrel lengths, and works around the mounting positions available in the game.

segments.summary: Once the main battery and basic protection fit, the remaining displacement and deck space must accommodate the modernized ship's secondary and anti-aircraft weapons.

segments.title: How one main-tower hit erases a fifteen-gun advantage
segments.body: The first battle test begins with fifteen British barrels against eight German ones, giving the Queen Elizabeth derivative a theoretical advantage in shell volume. A hit then destroys the main tower, leaving the ship unable to see the enemy properly even though the hull still reports about 95 percent structural integrity. Observation and fire-control positions matter as much as the number of guns mounted. A battleship can remain buoyant while losing the arrangements needed to turn its battery into effective fire. This failure drives the later rebuild.

evidence.note: He contrasts the fifteen-gun British broadside with Bismarck's eight guns, then loses the main tower and observes that the ship can no longer see the enemy despite retaining about 95 percent structural integrity.

segments.summary: The fifteen-gun Queen Elizabeth derivative has theoretical volume of fire, but an early hit destroys its main tower and leaves it unable to exploit that advantage.

segments.title: Could a fast pre-dreadnought escort a Second World War convoy?
segments.body: The answer separates a ship's escort value from its suitability for a line-of-battle fight. An early pre-dreadnought would be outclassed, while a later Lord Nelson-like design could still defeat a Deutschland or Panzerschiff type in the right circumstances. A speed of 23 to 25 knots could therefore be useful for convoy duty without making the ship suitable against an enemy battle fleet. The exchange judges an old warship by its assigned mission and likely opponent rather than age alone.

evidence.note: He contrasts convoy escort with fighting an enemy battle fleet and distinguishes early from late pre-dreadnoughts.

segments.summary: A 23- to 25-knot pre-dreadnought may be useful for convoy escort, but not for fighting a modern battle fleet.
segments.question: Could a pre-dreadnought making 23 to 25 knots serve in the Second World War?
segments.answerShort: Potentially as a convoy escort; an early type would not beat a modern battle fleet, but a later Lord Nelson-like ship could handle a Panzerschiff-type opponent.

segments.title: Rebuilding beam, topweight, and fire control after the first duel
segments.body: The first test ends once the vulnerable main tower and zero hit probability make the result uninformative. A wider hull makes room for a more substantial tower, followed by further adjustments to beam, machinery efficiency, and component placement. Moving equipment reduces the forward weight offset to roughly two percent, which should improve accuracy. Fire-control protection cannot be added independently because extra superstructure changes topweight, stability, propulsion efficiency, and the space available for secondary weapons. The rebuild turns the first battle's failure into a compact lesson in iterative naval architecture.

evidence.note: He stops the failed test, widens the hull to fit a stronger main tower, and adjusts beam, machinery efficiency, component position, and forward weight offset to improve the rebuilt ship's accuracy and balance.

segments.summary: The failed first duel sends the design back to the yard, where a wider hull and a stronger main tower must be balanced against machinery efficiency and forward weight.

segments.title: Giving the Bismarck model a fair historical allowance
segments.body: The game model is checked against Bismarck's historical 15-inch/51.6-calibre armament, along with its shell, explosive, protection, accommodation, and equipment settings. An implausible spacious-quarters allowance is removed and the bulkhead setting is reduced. The uncertain targeting system receives the modern option, giving the German design the benefit of the doubt. Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts still cannot provide a precise historical test, but these choices keep the counterfactual from depending on a hidden handicap.

evidence.note: He checks Bismarck's gun calibre, discusses model assumptions, and explains why he gives an uncertain opponent an equal or better allowance.

segments.summary: The ship-design comparison tries to model Bismarck at the best level German industry could plausibly support rather than handicapping the opponent.

segments.title: Keeping the fifth turret complicates aircraft handling
segments.body: The counterfactual keeps all five triple 16.5-inch turrets instead of following the Italian practice of removing a central turret during reconstruction. The standardized superstructure has hangar doors even though the ship lacks an aircraft-launch system. In principle the adjacent turret could be trained away to clear space, but every launch or recovery would then depend on moving the main battery. A retained turret can conflict with aviation facilities, funnels, secondary armament, and other refit requirements. Preserving the maximum gun count may therefore make a modernization less operationally coherent.

evidence.note: He keeps all five triple turrets, contrasts that choice with Italian removal of a fifth turret during upgrades, and explains why the hangar-door position would require moving the main battery to handle aircraft.

segments.summary: Retaining all five triple turrets preserves the fifteen-gun battery, but it crowds the refit and leaves the modeled hangar doors without a practical aircraft-launch arrangement.

segments.title: Why Bismarck's turtleback dominates the simulated duel
segments.body: Repeated heavy-gun fire produces little visible effect, and the modeled turtleback deck appears to be the reason Bismarck remains functional. Giving the British design the same scheme would test whether both ships could absorb punishment indefinitely. The experiment illustrates the protective logic of sloped internal armour and the danger of letting one game mechanic dominate a historical comparison. The design feature and the simulation's unusually strong implementation of it need to be judged separately.

evidence.note: He attributes the German ship's apparent immunity to the turtleback model and considers applying the same scheme to the British design as a test.

segments.summary: The game's turtleback model makes the German battleship extraordinarily hard to sink, raising a warning about translating simulated resilience directly into history.

segments.title: When fewer guns make a stronger battleship design
segments.body: The design experiment compares a fifteen-gun ship that cannot hit reliably with a twelve-gun alternative that can. Main-battery count is only one part of fighting power because fire control, stability, armour, and the ability to keep firing all shape the useful weight of fire. Bismarck should also close toward secondary range while its remaining 15-inch ammunition can still support the approach, making range control part of the endurance problem. Fewer barrels can be more valuable when the ship can find the target, stay intact, and use its ammunition under favourable tactical conditions.

evidence.note: He considers removing the central turret for more superstructure, explains why twelve hitting guns can be better than fifteen missing guns, and argues that Bismarck should close before exhausting its 15-inch ammunition.

segments.summary: A conversion that removes a turret may be preferable when it frees weight for fire control, protection, and a more accurate ship.

segments.title: A zero-aim bug invalidates the first gunnery result
segments.body: The first duel's British fire-control performance falls to a displayed zero percent chance to hit even as the range closes. A viewer identifies a reported bug, confirming that Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts is unsuitable for this accuracy test. The battle cannot serve as a clean comparison of British and German gunnery systems. It remains useful as a design visualization, although the bug invalidates its numerical gunnery result.

evidence.note: The British ship shows a zero percent hit chance, a viewer identifies the reported zero-aim bug, and Dr. Clarke says this is why he uses Harpoon rather than UAD for testing.

segments.summary: A reported zero-aim bug makes the first duel unusable as a precision gunnery test and explains why Harpoon is reserved for accuracy-focused work.

segments.title: Why a British-German battleship duel signals a wider failure
segments.body: A one-on-one engagement is an exceptional and undesirable situation for Britain rather than the normal purpose of fleet strategy. Such a duel means much has gone wrong on the British side unless a ship such as Renown or Rodney has independently found the opponent. The point shifts attention from isolated ship statistics to the operational circumstances that produce contact. A one-on-one simulation does not represent the Royal Navy's normal way of seeking a decisive action.

evidence.note: He says a British and German battleship fighting alone means much has gone wrong for Britain, with Renown and Rodney as exceptions.

segments.summary: A lone British-German capital-ship duel is usually a sign that the Royal Navy's wider operational advantages have broken down.

segments.title: Winning because the enemy exhausts its main-battery ammunition
segments.body: The German ammunition count falls to only a few salvos and then reaches zero. Once the 15-inch battery is silent, the British ship can close and inflict damage with its remaining weapons. The result does not prove that the British design is superior because victory comes from the opponent's ammunition expenditure and the British ship's ability to keep firing. Ammunition capacity and fire discipline therefore belong beside nominal firepower, accuracy, protection, and endurance in the comparison.

evidence.note: He counts down the German main-battery ammunition and says the British victory resulted from the opponent running out of shells rather than from a better ship design.

segments.summary: The first duel becomes a lesson in ammunition endurance when Bismarck expends its main-battery shells before destroying the badly damaged British ship.

segments.title: The 14-inch gun Dreadnought that might have changed the arms race
segments.body: The industrial choice was available in 1905 because Elswick's 14-inch/45-calibre weapon existed while Dreadnought was being planned. The real design reused 12-inch gun and turret machinery associated with the Lord Nelson class, reducing cost and protecting the rapid construction schedule. Choosing the larger weapon might have delayed entry into service, although that delay is uncertain. The immediate procurement trade-off leads into the wider arms-race consequences developed in the following discussion.

evidence.note: He says Elswick's 14-inch/45-calibre gun was available during Dreadnought's planning, contrasts it with the reused Lord Nelson 12-inch turrets, and notes the possible construction delay.

segments.summary: Elswick's 14-inch gun was available when Dreadnought was planned, but the historical ship reused Lord Nelson 12-inch turrets to save time and money.
segments.question: What if Britain had begun the dreadnought era with a 14-inch-gun design rather than the historical Dreadnought?
segments.answerShort: The larger gun was available and would have made Dreadnought more powerful, but adopting it traded the proven Lord Nelson turret shortcut for possible cost and schedule delay.

segments.title: A five-triple-turret Dreadnought before the dreadnought race
segments.body: Fisher initially doubted whether one turret could fire safely over another, but later accepted that the arrangement was possible. The counterfactual gives a 1905-06 Dreadnought five triple 14-inch turrets, a fifteen-gun broadside, and six guns able to fire ahead. Such a ship would resemble an Orion-generation design years early and make twin-turret 12-inch contemporaries look obsolete before they entered service. Germany would have to answer a 14-inch standard instead of defending its 11-inch guns as equivalent to British 12-inch weapons, slowing any matching construction while Britain began follow-on ships. This enlarged lead might have reduced the intensity of the arms race and better served Fisher's deterrent purpose, although that remains a counterfactual argument rather than a prediction.

evidence.note: He discusses Fisher's view of superfiring, imagines a five-triple-14-inch Dreadnought built in 1905–06, and follows its effects through German construction, Britain's building lead, and deterrence.

segments.summary: Combining superfiring turrets with 14-inch guns would have made the first Dreadnought resemble an Orion-era ship years early and widened Britain's opening lead.

segments.title: What the twelve-gun reconstruction gains from better fire control
segments.body: The rebuilt design carries twelve rather than fifteen 16.5-inch guns and uses the released space and weight for a stronger fire-control arrangement. In the next duel it begins landing effective fire while remaining comparatively intact, turning the earlier theoretical trade-off into an observable result. The outcome is not automatic because the British ship closes before Bismarck's remaining ammunition has been sufficiently reduced and exposes itself to avoidable return fire. Reconstruction choices and tactical judgment both shape the gunnery result.

evidence.note: He notes the added secondary fire-control system and improved battle performance, then explains that closing while Bismarck still had about twenty-five salvos was premature.

segments.summary: Removing the central turret and adding a secondary fire-control position produces a far more effective ship, although closing the range too early still creates danger.

segments.title: How an 18-inch Argincourt could reshape naval treaties
segments.body: The discussion treats an 18-inch Argincourt as a technology shock rather than simply a stronger British ship. An imagined entry into service around 1914-16, after German construction had ceased matching Britain's pace, would establish a new global benchmark. American and Japanese designers would then have strong incentives to pursue comparable ships of their own. Later capital-ship choices might revolve around an 18-inch super-heavy, a rapid-fire 16-inch ship, or a 14-inch quad-turret alternative, changing the background to naval limitation agreements.

evidence.note: He considers an 18-inch Argincourt, likely American and Japanese reactions, treaty consequences, and later gun-calibre choices.

segments.summary: An 18-inch-gun Argincourt would likely provoke American and Japanese replies and make later treaty limits far harder to negotiate.

segments.title: How larger capital ships could raise the cruiser calibre ceiling
segments.body: The answer projects the consequences of a more heavily armed Queen Elizabeth class and an 18-inch Argincourt. Hawkins might have moved beyond 7.5-inch guns, with 9.2 inches a more plausible practical ceiling than an attempted 10-inch cruiser gun. Treaty categories and ship roles depend on relative fighting power because a capital ship only slightly more heavily armed than a cruiser loses much of its rationale. Changing the capital-ship benchmark could therefore alter cruiser design and the definitions used in naval-limitation agreements.

evidence.note: He answers a question about alternate-timeline cruisers, Hawkins armament, and the relationship between cruiser and capital-ship gun calibres.

segments.summary: A world of 18-inch capital ships could make 9.2- or 10-inch cruisers more attractive while making 12-inch battleships look inadequate.
segments.question: How might cruiser designs change if this alternate timeline produced much larger-gunned capital ships?
segments.answerShort: Cruisers might plausibly move to 9.2-inch guns, while 12-inch battleships would lose credibility if a cruiser could approach their firepower.

segments.title: Why losing oilers can wreck a Pacific campaign
segments.body: The short exchange makes logistics the decisive issue in a Pacific operational game. A damaged or lost carrier is serious, but an oiler shortage can prevent the force from reaching, sustaining, or withdrawing from its intended area of operations. Combat power depends on the fuel network that lets a fleet move across the theatre. Naval power therefore rests on replenishment ships as well as combatants.

evidence.note: He says a carrier loss is annoying in War in the Pacific, but losing oilers is the operational problem because logistics always governs.

segments.summary: Fleet oilers matter so much in the Pacific that losing them can be more damaging to operations than losing a carrier.

segments.title: Designing Conqueror as a twelve-gun 18-inch fast battleship
segments.body: After Argincourt's erratic test, a separate Conqueror concept is built with twelve 18-inch guns. Beam and draft are narrowed around a 28-knot requirement while pitch, roll, and fore-and-aft weight shift change with the hull. The gun model is reduced from an implausible 48- or 49-calibre length toward 45 calibres, and armour and internal protection absorb the tonnage recovered elsewhere. Enhanced or semi-automatic loading offers more firepower but creates another weight choice, while an all-or-nothing protection scheme receives a direct test. This is a counterfactual design exercise rather than a claim that such a ship existed, and each improvement forces a concession in stability, protection, machinery, or weapons.

evidence.note: He starts the Conqueror test with twelve 18-inch guns, a 28-knot target, and repeated beam, draft, pitch, roll, and weight-distribution adjustments.
He settles the gun model toward 45 calibres, trades armour and loading arrangements against weight, and selects all-or-nothing protection before launching the test.

segments.summary: A second counterfactual turns the 18-inch concept into a 28-knot, twelve-gun design whose hull form, gun length, protection, and loading system must fit one displacement budget.

segments.title: Why the stream treats UAD as exploration rather than a precision test
segments.body: A question about sharing ship designs leads into what the game contributes to these historical experiments. Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts is enjoyable and fast enough for building counterfactual ships and watching their trade-offs play out. It is described as a quick-and-dirty tool, while Harpoon is reserved for accuracy testing. This caveat applies to every battle result in the stream: the simulations prompt design analysis but do not provide controlled historical proof.

evidence.note: While discussing shared designs, he says he uses Harpoon for accuracy testing and Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts because it is fun and quick-and-dirty.

segments.summary: The answer distinguishes the quick visual experiments of Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts from the Harpoon system reserved for accuracy-focused testing.
segments.question: Are the ship designs from these streams available to share or review?
segments.answerShort: A way to share UAD designs is still being investigated; the game is useful for quick visual experiments, while Harpoon remains the tool for accuracy-focused testing.

segments.title: The procurement weakness behind German naval radar
segments.body: The comparison gives the German ship the weaker radar arrangement. German naval sets are characterized as one-off, bespoke models and contrasted with a factory-production approach. The problem is institutional as much as technical because repeated custom solutions make integration, support, and improvement harder than standardization. Sensor performance therefore depends partly on procurement policy rather than on an isolated equipment statistic.

evidence.note: He contrasts the radar sets and characterizes German naval radar procurement as a succession of bespoke one-off systems.

segments.summary: German naval radar suffered from bespoke, one-off procurement choices rather than a consistent production approach.

segments.title: What an 18-inch hit means for a battleship
segments.body: The danger of an 18-inch gun depends on whether its shells hit. Yamato and Musashi provide the examples: a battleship might endure an isolated 18-inch strike but would struggle to remain effective under repeated hits. The game's damage behaviour cannot quantify a real shell's effect, especially after the stream's earlier modelling problems. The sequence separates shell power from the fire-control reliability needed to deliver it.

evidence.note: He discusses 18-inch hits, Yamato and Musashi, and distinguishes an isolated hit from repeated successful strikes.

segments.summary: The stream uses Yamato and Musashi to underline the destructive potential of 18-inch shells once they strike a target.

segments.title: Why a floating battleship may no longer be a fighting battleship
segments.body: The damaged German ship remains fast and able to fire despite a heavy list, water sweeping over the hull, damaged engines, and the loss of much of its ammunition. Staying afloat is different from retaining useful fighting power because firing heavy guns at such an angle would worsen the list, while machinery damage should reduce speed. The design's quantity of steel is compared with the N3 concept before it absorbs repeated 18-inch hits and continues scoring improbably accurate broadsides in a tight turn. Structural buoyancy, mobility, weapon operation, and combat effectiveness are separate thresholds of survivability. The eventual sinking does not validate the combat behaviour that preceded it. A game's final sinking time cannot by itself measure historical resilience.

evidence.note: He explains why the flooding, list, ammunition loss, and damaged engines should prevent the ship from fighting or maintaining speed even if it remains afloat.
He compares the design's steel with N3, then criticizes its ability to absorb repeated 18-inch hits, remain afloat, and keep scoring broadsides while turning under a severe list.

segments.summary: Severe flooding, list, machinery damage, and ammunition loss should destroy combat effectiveness well before a battleship finally sinks.
